To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the net effect of clouds is a cooling of the climate system, and that this effect is dominated by longwave cooling at the top of atmosphere, but that the effect on the surface is dominated by shortwave warming.

the global annual mean cloud forcing (i.e., the difference between all-sky and cloud-free radiation fluxes at the TOA) is about –20 Wm−2, with the largest negative forcing in the tropics and the largest positive forcing in the midlatitudes, and that the cloud feedback in climate model simulations is positive.
the global mean annual radiative effect of clouds is a cooling of 21 W/m2, and that the cloud feedback in climate model simulations is a warming of 3.4 W/m2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.

the following: 1) the radiative effects of the cloud cover, including its diurnal and annual variations, and its effect on climate; and 2) a study of the role of the cloud cover in climate change, including the feedbacks of clouds on climate and the effect of climate on clouds.

the following topics: the impact of clouds and aerosols on radiative flux divergence and on the energy balance at the top of atmosphere (TOA) the impact of cloud and aerosol radiative effects on climate feedbacks the impact of clouds, aerosols and other variables on the hydrologic cycle, and on the water budget at the top of and within the atmosphere.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the net effect of clouds on climate is to cool the planet, but that there are large uncertainties in the magnitude of the effect and in the way it is distributed spatially and seasonally.
the net effect of clouds on the climate system is to cool it, but that the magnitude of the effect is uncertain.
the total effect of clouds, as measured by the cloud forcing, has a cooling effect of 21.3 Wm−2 on the annual global mean radiation budget.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
clouds have a net cooling effect on the Earth's radiation budget.
the net effect of clouds is a cooling of the Earth's climate system, and that this cooling is due to the combined effects of clouds on both the incoming and outgoing longwave radiation.

clouds are a major factor in the climate system, exerting a strong influence on the radiation budget, and that they have an important two-way interaction with other climate variables, especially the hydrological cycle and the surface temperature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
clouds have a net cooling effect on climate, but the magnitude of the effect varies significantly depending on the climate model used.
, while there are some differences in the details, the results from different studies are in good overall agreement.
the climate system is a complex system and we need to understand the interactions between clouds and other variables of the system.
